subChunks.title: Particle Physics & the Standard Model
subChunks.hookHtml:
Theodora projected a single image onto the board: a dense tableau of particles arranged into rows and columns — the Standard Model. “Humanity’s deepest answer to ‘what is everything made of?’” she said. “Seventeen fundamental particles. Three of the four fundamental forces. An equation that fits on a T-shirt and predicts experimental results to twelve decimal places.” She paused. “And yet. No gravity. No dark matter. No dark energy. No explanation for why there is more matter than antimatter in the universe. The Standard Model is the most successful theory in the history of science — and we know it is incomplete.”

Particle physics probes matter at its smallest scale by smashing particles together at extraordinary energies and watching what emerges. The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN collides protons at energies up to 13.6 TeV — energies not seen in the universe since fractions of a second after the Big Bang. The Higgs boson, detected at CERN in 2012, was the final missing piece of the Standard Model, confirming a prediction first made in 1964. Its discovery was not the end of particle physics; it opened new questions about why the Higgs mass is what it is, and why the universe did not annihilate itself at the Big Bang.

At SENIOR level, you are expected to classify particles correctly, understand the roles of forces and their mediating bosons, apply conservation laws, and critically evaluate what the Standard Model explains and what lies genuinely beyond it.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Fundamental Particles — Fermions

Matter particles are fermions — they have half-integer spin (1/2) and obey the Pauli Exclusion Principle. Fermions divide into two families:

Quarks (6 types, or “flavours”): up (u), down (d), charm (c), strange (s), top (t), bottom (b). Quarks have fractional electric charges (+2/3 or −1/3) and carry a property called colour charge (red, green, blue — an analogy, not a real colour). Quarks cannot exist in isolation — they are always “confined” inside composite particles called hadrons. Baryons (e.g. protons, neutrons) contain three quarks; mesons contain one quark and one antiquark. A proton is two up quarks and one down quark (uud), giving charge +1. A neutron is udd, giving charge 0.

Leptons (6 types): electron (e⁻), muon (μ⁻), tau (τ⁻), electron neutrino (νₑ), muon neutrino (νμ), tau neutrino (ντ). Leptons do not carry colour charge and are not subject to the strong force. The electron is stable; the muon and tau are heavier, unstable, and decay to lighter leptons. Neutrinos are near-massless, carry only weak charge, and interact only via the weak force and gravity — making them extraordinarily difficult to detect.

Every fermion has an antiparticle with opposite charge but identical mass. The electron’s antiparticle is the positron (e⁺); the antiproton contains two anti-up and one anti-down quark. Matter and antimatter annihilate on contact, releasing energy via E=2mc² (for particle-antiparticle pairs at rest).

Fundamental Particles — Bosons

Gauge bosons mediate the fundamental forces (integer spin, obey Bose-Einstein statistics):

  • Photon (γ): Mediates the electromagnetic force. Massless, charge-neutral, infinite range. Electric charges interact by exchanging virtual photons.
  • W⁺, W⁻, Z⁰ bosons: Mediate the weak nuclear force, responsible for radioactive beta decay. Massive (~80–91 GeV/c²) — which is why the weak force has very short range (~10⁻¹⁸ m). W bosons change quark flavour (e.g. neutron β⁻ decay: d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ via W⁻ emission).
  • Gluons (8 types): Mediate the strong force, binding quarks together inside hadrons and protons/neutrons together in nuclei. Massless but colour-charged — gluons interact with each other (unlike photons). This self-interaction creates quark confinement: separating quarks requires increasingly large energy, eventually producing new quark-antiquark pairs rather than free quarks.

The Higgs boson (H⁰): The quantum excitation of the Higgs field, which permeates all space. Particles acquire mass by interacting with this field — the stronger the interaction, the more massive the particle. Photons and gluons, which do not interact with the Higgs field, remain massless. The Higgs boson itself has a mass of ~125 GeV/c². It was predicted in 1964 (Peter Higgs, among others) and detected at CERN’s LHC in 2012 by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations.

The Four Fundamental Forces

ForceCarrierRelative StrengthRangeActs On
Strong nuclearGluons1~10⁻¹⁵ mQuarks, gluons
ElectromagneticPhoton~1/137InfiniteCharged particles
Weak nuclearW±, Z⁰~10⁻⁶~10⁻¹⁸ mAll fermions
GravityGraviton(?)~10⁻³⁸InfiniteAll particles with mass/energy

Gravity is not described by the Standard Model. The hypothetical graviton (spin-2 boson) has not been detected, and no consistent quantum theory of gravity exists.

Conservation Laws

Particle interactions must conserve:

  • Energy-momentum (always)
  • Electric charge (always)
  • Baryon number (B — number of quarks/3; conserved in all known interactions)
  • Lepton number (Le, Lμ, Lτ — conserved separately in most interactions; violated by neutrino oscillations)
  • Colour charge (in strong interactions — all hadrons are “colour neutral”)

Some quantum numbers are conserved only in certain interactions. Strangeness, charm, and bottom quantum numbers are conserved by the strong and electromagnetic forces but are violated by the weak force — which is why strange particles decay via the weak force and have relatively long lifetimes.

Beta Decay — A Detailed Example

Neutron beta minus decay (n → p⁺ + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ) is mediated by the weak force at the quark level: a down quark in the neutron emits a virtual W⁻ boson and becomes an up quark. The W⁻ then decays to an electron and an electron antineutrino. Conservation checks: charge (0 → +1−1+0 = 0 ✓), baryon number (1 → 1+0+0 = 1 ✓), lepton number (0 → 0+1−1 = 0 ✓, where antineutrino has Lₑ = −1).

Symmetries and the Standard Model

The Standard Model is formulated as a gauge theory based on the symmetry group SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1). The strong force is described by quantum chromodynamics (QCD); the electromagnetic and weak forces are unified into electroweak theory (Glashow-Weinberg-Salam model, Nobel Prize 1979). At very high energies (above ~100 GeV), the electromagnetic and weak forces appear as a single electroweak force — they are spontaneously broken into distinct forces at lower energies by the Higgs mechanism.

Beyond the Standard Model — Open Questions

The Standard Model is spectacularly successful but demonstrably incomplete:

  • Dark matter: ~27% of the universe’s energy density is non-luminous, non-baryonic matter. No Standard Model particle fits. Leading candidates include WIMPs (weakly interacting massive particles) and axions, but none have been directly detected.
  • Matter-antimatter asymmetry (baryogenesis): The Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter; their annihilation should have left a universe of pure radiation. The observed asymmetry (roughly one extra baryon per billion annihilations) requires CP violation beyond what the Standard Model predicts.
  • Neutrino masses: The Standard Model predicts massless neutrinos. Neutrino oscillations (flavour changes between types) demonstrate they have small but non-zero masses. This requires physics beyond the Standard Model.
  • The hierarchy problem: The Higgs mass (~125 GeV) is unnaturally small compared to the Planck scale (~10¹⁹ GeV) — quantum corrections should make it enormous unless there is fine-tuned cancellation. Supersymmetry (SUSY) and extra dimensions have been proposed but not confirmed by the LHC.
  • Quantum gravity: Gravity is not included. The Standard Model breaks down at the Planck scale.

storyBeats.text: Theodora drew a proton on the board — two up quarks and a down quark, surrounded by gluons. “A proton weighs about 938 MeV. The quarks themselves account for only about 1% of that mass. The remaining 99% comes from the kinetic energy of quarks and gluons flying around inside. The proton is almost all energy.”
“So when we say a proton has mass, we’re mostly talking about confined energy? And the Higgs gives mass to the quarks themselves, not to the proton?”

“Exactly. The Higgs field gives the quarks their rest mass — a few MeV each. The proton’s mass is dominated by QCD binding energy, not the Higgs. If you want to understand why things weigh what they do, you need both.”
“And the hierarchy problem — why is the Higgs mass 125 GeV when it ‘should’ be near the Planck scale? Is that just a calculation issue?”

“It’s a genuine puzzle. Quantum field theory predicts virtual particles contribute enormous corrections to the Higgs mass. For the observed value to emerge, those corrections must cancel to extraordinary precision — about one part in 10³⁰. That level of fine-tuning strikes most physicists as unnatural. SUSY was supposed to solve this by introducing partner particles that cancel the corrections automatically. The LHC has not found SUSY particles where theory predicted they should be.”

“The Standard Model fits on a T-shirt. But the T-shirt has seventeen unknown parameters — the particle masses, coupling constants — that the theory does not explain: they are inputs from experiment. A truly fundamental theory would derive them. We do not have that theory yet.”

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what quarks are, why we cannot see them individually, and what evidence we have that they actually exist inside protons and neutrons. Assume no prior knowledge of particle physics.
learningObjectives: Classify fundamental particles as quarks, leptons, or gauge bosons and state the charge, spin, and role of each
Apply conservation laws (charge, baryon number, lepton number) to determine whether a proposed particle interaction or decay is permitted
Explain the role of the Higgs field in mass generation and distinguish what the Higgs mechanism explains from what it does not
Critically evaluate the status of the Standard Model — identifying at least four phenomena it successfully predicts and four it cannot account for
commonMistakes: Describing gluons as massless and therefore the strong force should have infinite range — the confinement of colour charge inside hadrons limits the force’s effective range to ~10⁻¹⁵ m, unlike the photon’s case
Thinking the Higgs boson gives all particles their mass — it gives elementary particles their rest mass, but composite particles like the proton get ~99% of their mass from QCD binding energy
Confusing hadrons (composite quark structures) with fundamental particles — protons and neutrons are made of quarks and are not fundamental

Stating that the Standard Model has been proven by the Higgs discovery — the Higgs confirmed a prediction but the SM still has severe known limitations (dark matter, neutrino masses, gravity, baryogenesis)
assessmentCriteria: Can classify any given particle (proton, electron, photon, neutrino, pion, etc.) correctly using the Standard Model taxonomy
Can work through a decay process applying all relevant conservation laws and identify which force mediates it
Can explain the Higgs mechanism at a conceptual level and identify what questions it resolves and what it leaves open
Can critically discuss the experimental status of beyond-Standard-Model physics, including what the LHC has and has not found
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Consider the following proposed particle interactions or decays. For each one, determine whether it is permitted under the Standard Model by checking the relevant conservation laws. State which law is violated (if any), and identify which force mediates the interaction if it is permitted.

  1. n → p⁺ + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ (neutron beta-minus decay)
  2. p⁺ → e⁺ + γ (proton decays to a positron and a photon)
  3. μ⁻ → e⁻ + ν̄ₑ + νμ (muon decay)
  4. e⁻ + e⁺ → 2γ (electron-positron annihilation)
  5. u + ū → g (up quark and anti-up quark produce a single gluon)
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. n → p⁺ + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ:
Charge: 0 → +1−1+0 = 0 ✓
Baryon: 1 → 1+0+0 = 1 ✓
Lepton (electron): 0 → 0+1−1 = 0 ✓ (antineutrino carries Lₑ = −1)
Permitted. Mediated by the weak force (W⁻ boson): d → u + W⁻, then W⁻ → e⁻ + ν̄ₑ.

2. p⁺ → e⁺ + γ:
Charge: +1 → +1+0 = +1 ✓
Baryon: 1 → 0+0 = 0 ✗
Violated: baryon number not conserved. Not permitted by Standard Model. (Note: some beyond-SM theories predict proton decay via different modes, but the SM forbids it. The current experimental lower bound on proton lifetime is >10³⁴ years.)

3. μ⁻ → e⁻ + ν̄ₑ + νμ:
Charge: −1 → −1+0+0 = −1 ✓
Baryon: 0 → 0 ✓
Electron lepton: 0 → 1−1+0 = 0 ✓ (ν̄ₑ carries Lₑ = −1)
Muon lepton: 1 → 0+0+1 = 1 ✓
Permitted. Mediated by the weak force (W⁻ boson). This is the standard muon decay mode.

4. e⁻ + e⁺ → 2γ:
Charge: −1+1 = 0 → 0+0 = 0 ✓
Baryon: 0 → 0 ✓
Lepton: 1−1 = 0 → 0 ✓
Energy/momentum: two photons can carry away total energy (2mc² in rest frame) ✓
Permitted. Mediated by the electromagnetic force. This is pair annihilation — the positron is the electron’s antiparticle, total lepton number is zero.

5. u + ū → g (single gluon):
Colour charge: a quark-antiquark pair can be colour-neutral (colour singlet). A single gluon carries colour-anticolour charge — it is not colour-neutral. The system would need to produce a colour-neutral state externally.
More fundamentally, producing a single on-shell gluon violates momentum-energy conservation in the centre-of-mass frame (a single massless particle cannot absorb a massive system’s energy and momentum simultaneously). In practice, u+ū annihilate to produce a gluon jet or other colour-neutral hadrons.
Not permitted as written. Single isolated gluons cannot exist — colour confinement requires colour-neutral final states.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: The LHC discovered the Higgs boson in 2012, confirming the last major prediction of the Standard Model. Some commentators described this as “the end of particle physics” — the final piece of the puzzle found. Others argued it was the beginning of a new era of uncertainty. Evaluate both perspectives, drawing on: (a) what the Higgs discovery actually confirmed and what questions it raised; (b) the status of beyond-Standard-Model searches at the LHC; (c) the open questions the Standard Model cannot address; and (d) what “progress” in fundamental physics looks like when predictions are confirmed but deeper puzzles remain.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a) What the Higgs discovery confirmed and what it raised:
The Higgs discovery confirmed the electroweak symmetry-breaking mechanism predicted by Higgs, Brout, Englert, and others in 1964 — the last major untested prediction of the Standard Model. The measured mass (~125 GeV/c²) and decay channels matched predictions. However, the discovery immediately raised questions: Why is the Higgs mass 125 GeV and not near the Planck scale (the hierarchy problem)? Is the Higgs elementary or composite? Are there multiple Higgs bosons (as supersymmetric theories predict)? The discovery was a culmination and a starting point simultaneously.

(b) Status of BSM searches at the LHC:
The LHC at 13-13.6 TeV has searched extensively for signatures of physics beyond the Standard Model: supersymmetric particles, extra dimensions, micro-black holes, dark matter candidates. As of the mid-2020s, none have been found. This absence is significant — it rules out large swathes of parameter space for popular BSM theories, particularly “natural” SUSY at low masses. The LHC has not ended particle physics; it has excluded many proposed solutions and forced theorists to revisit assumptions. High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) upgrades will continue probing — but the era of confident BSM prediction has been humbled.

(c) Open questions the SM cannot address:
Dark matter (~27% of universe’s energy density) — no SM particle fits gravitational lensing, galaxy rotation, and CMB constraints. Dark energy (~68%) — entirely unexplained. Matter-antimatter asymmetry — the observed excess of matter requires more CP violation than the SM provides. Neutrino masses — SM predicts zero; oscillations prove otherwise. Gravity — the SM has no graviton, no quantum gravity. The hierarchy problem — unresolved. The SM also has ~17 free parameters with no deeper explanation. Calling its completion “the end” ignores that it describes only 5% of the universe’s content.

(d) What progress looks like here:
The history of physics shows that confirming a theory often reveals its limits most clearly. Maxwell’s unification of electricity and magnetism led to relativity. Quantum mechanics emerged from the failure of classical physics to explain blackbody radiation. Similarly, the Higgs discovery complete a theoretical framework that is demonstrably insufficient. Progress in this regime may look different from earlier eras — predictions have become harder to test because the energy scales of suspected new physics may be inaccessible to near-term colliders. This raises genuine methodological questions: Are we entering a post-empirical phase in physics? Most physicists resist that conclusion, arguing that future experiments — neutrino oscillation measurements, dark matter searches, gravitational wave observatories, proposed future colliders — will eventually probe new physics. The Higgs discovery was not an end; it was a sharply illuminated gap.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The quantum field theory describing the strong nuclear force, formulated in terms of colour charge carried by quarks and gluons — the SU(3) sector of the Standard Model. Asymptotic freedom (quarks behave nearly free at high energies) was recognised with the 2004 Nobel Prize.

Graphical representations of perturbative calculations in quantum field theory — each diagram corresponds to a mathematical term in a series expansion of interaction amplitudes, making particle physics calculations tractable and visualisable.

Violation of the combined symmetry of charge conjugation (C, swapping particles for antiparticles) and parity (P, mirroring spatial coordinates). CP violation is observed in kaon and B-meson systems and is necessary for baryogenesis, but the SM predicts too little of it.

The quantum mechanical phenomenon where a neutrino created as one flavour (e.g. electron neutrino) oscillates between flavours as it propagates — demonstrating that neutrinos have non-zero (but tiny) masses, in conflict with the original Standard Model.

A theoretical extension of the Standard Model that proposes every fermion has a boson ‘superpartner’ and vice versa — which would resolve the hierarchy problem and provide dark matter candidates (the lightest supersymmetric particle). No SUSY particles have been found at the LHC.

Mathematical functions describing the probability of finding a particular quark or gluon (parton) carrying a given fraction of a proton’s momentum — essential for predicting LHC collision outcomes since proton constituents carry varying momentum fractions.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following correctly identifies the quark content of a neutron?
options: One up quark and two down quarks (udd)
Two up quarks and one down quark (uud)
questions.correctAnswer: One up quark and two down quarks (udd)
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. A neutron has quark content udd: charge = +2/3 − 1/3 − 1/3 = 0. It has baryon number 1 (three quarks each contributing 1/3).

questions.questionHtml: In neutron beta-minus decay, a down quark converts to an up quark. Which boson mediates this conversion, and to what particles does it subsequently decay?
options: A W⁻ boson, which decays to an electron and an electron antineutrino
A Z⁰ boson, which decays to an electron and an electron neutrino
A gluon, which decays to an electron and a positron
A W⁺ boson, which decays to a positron and an electron neutrino
questions.correctAnswer: A W⁻ boson, which decays to an electron and an electron antineutrino
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. The process is d → u + W⁻, then W⁻ → e⁻ + ν̄ₑ. The W⁻ is the weak-force carrier for charge-changing interactions. Charge is conserved: −1/3 → +2/3 + (−1) for the virtual W⁻, which then decays to −1 + 0 for the electron and antineutrino.

questions.questionHtml: The LHC has not discovered supersymmetric particles at the energies searched so far. A student concludes: “This proves supersymmetry is wrong — the Standard Model is complete.” Identify the most significant flaw in this reasoning.
options: Absence of evidence at currently accessible energies excludes specific low-mass SUSY parameter space but does not prove SUSY is incorrect across all masses, and the Standard Model is demonstrably incomplete regardless of SUSY’s status
The LHC cannot prove any theory wrong because particle accelerators only create, not detect, particles
Supersymmetry was never a prediction of the Standard Model, so its absence cannot confirm or deny the Standard Model’s completeness
SUSY has been confirmed at CERN but the results have not yet been published
questions.correctAnswer: Absence of evidence at currently accessible energies excludes specific low-mass SUSY parameter space but does not prove SUSY is incorrect across all masses, and the Standard Model is demonstrably incomplete regardless of SUSY’s status
questions.explanationHtml: Correct. The LHC rules out SUSY particles below certain mass thresholds — not SUSY universally. SUSY particles could exist at higher masses the LHC cannot reach. Separately, the Standard Model cannot explain dark matter, neutrino masses, matter-antimatter asymmetry, or gravity — it is incomplete regardless of whether SUSY is correct.
